analysis.one_liner: Makes public college tuition-free and cancels all outstanding student loans.
analysis.headline: Not a single senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill to make public college free and wipe out all federal student debt died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made tuition and fees free at community colleges, public four-year colleges, and tribal colleges, with federal grants covering about two-thirds of the cost and states about a third. It would also have canceled every outstanding federal student loan — including parent and consolidation loans — bought out and forgiven private student loans, and capped new federal loan interest at 1.88%. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every federal student loan borrower would have had their principal and interest erased within 180 days of enactment, tax-free — including parent borrowers, consolidation loans, and grants that had been converted to loans [S2][S3]. Borrowers with private student loans could apply to have the Education Department buy the loan from the lender and forgive it [S3]. Students at community colleges, public four-year colleges, and tribal colleges would pay no tuition or required fees, and low-income students at private historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions would see tuition eliminated or sharply reduced [S2]. New federal student loans would be capped at a 1.88% interest rate [S3]. The bill also expands work-study (from $1.5 billion toward $3.5 billion a year) and steers it toward colleges serving low-income students, plus larger TRIO and GEAR UP programs for first-generation and low-income students [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student borrowers and public college students

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges, public four-year institutions, and tribal colleges, through federal grants covering 67% of the cost and requiring states to put up 33% from their own funds

Cancels the full outstanding principal and interest on every federal student loan within 180 days of enactment, including parent loans, consolidation loans, and grants treated as loans, and makes the forgiveness tax-free; borrowers who paid between enactment and forgiveness get refunds
Lets borrowers with private student loans apply to have the Education Department purchase the loan — paying the lender principal, accrued interest, and late charges — and then forgive it, tax-free
Caps interest on new federal student loans — undergraduate, graduate, PLUS, and consolidation — at 1.88%

Funds grants for private, nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions to eliminate or significantly reduce tuition for low-income students, with $1.34 billion authorized for fiscal 2020

Expands Federal Work-Study funding and rewires its formula to direct money to colleges that enroll low-income and moderate-income students, and increases TRIO and GEAR UP funding for low-income and first-generation students

Attaches strings that push colleges toward students rather than administration: states and colleges must maintain instruction spending and need-based aid at 2017-18 levels, cover the full cost of attendance for students with maximum Pell Grants, move to at least 75% tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years, and cannot use the money on stadiums, administrator salaries, or merit aid

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through direct appropriations: $48 billion for fiscal 2020 plus 'such sums as may be necessary' for every year through 2029, and full loan forgiveness, with no tax or offsetting revenue specified anywhere in the bill text [S3]. States would fund a 33% non-federal share of tuition costs and must keep higher-education spending at 2017-18 levels [S3]. The Department of Education would give up the loan assets it holds, and private lenders would be paid off at full value including accrued interest and late charges [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill never says where the money comes from: it appropriates $48 billion for fiscal 2020 plus 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2029 and forgives all federal loans, with no tax, fee, or offset written into the bill

Because forgiveness is universal, it would erase large graduate-school and parent loans for higher-income households on the same terms as small loans for low-income borrowers, so a large share of the money would flow to people who least need help

Private student lenders would be paid the full unpaid principal, accrued interest, and even late charges on the loans the government buys out — no loss shared by the lenders who charged students the highest rates
States must fund 33% of tuition costs and lock in 2017-18 spending on instruction and need-based aid to qualify, which could strain state budgets or pressure other programs

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is about as large as a single education bill gets: total debt cancellation for every federal borrower and free tuition at public colleges, with real strings forcing colleges to spend on instruction and low-income students. The design flaws are real — no funding source is specified, forgiveness is not means-tested, and private lenders are made whole down to their late fees. A serious version would have needed a revenue title and tighter targeting. None of that was ever negotiated, because the bill never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the College for All Act of 2019 on June 24, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day
The Senate Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never came to the Senate floor
Over its entire life in Congress, no senator from either party joined as a cosponsor
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no vote ever taken in either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and private lenders kept their portfolios and revenue, and the federal government kept collecting on every federal student loan. Borrowers received nothing, and no college got new funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and zero senators from either party cosponsored the bill, so it never drew a partisan test in the record.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and collection agencies
industries.note: Forgiving every federal loan would have eliminated the servicing and collection revenue tied to that debt. Their interest runs against borrowers keeping their balances.

The bill would buy existing private loans at full value — principal, accrued interest, and late charges — so lenders take no loss, but they lose the future interest stream on those loans. They profit from high-rate lending to students who cannot otherwise cover costs.

Federal grants would permanently replace tuition as the funding source for public higher education, with strings attached: maintenance-of-effort, full-cost aid for maximum-Pell students, and a 75% tenured-faculty requirement. Revenue becomes guaranteed, and the institutions become a permanent federal funding channel.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: A new $1.34 billion-a-year grant stream (fiscal 2020) to eliminate or sharply cut tuition for their low-income students, with limits on tuition hikes.

The bill excludes for-profit institutions from the new grant programs, and even institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status are barred for 25 years, while free public tuition would pull their prospective students away.
